Key Characteristics & Etiology: Common bile duct stone or stricture with enteric bacterial infection (E. coli, Klebsiella).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Biliary stasis and increased intraductal pressure leading to bacterial translocation into systemic circulation.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Charcot's Triad (RUQ pain, fever with rigors, jaundice); Reynolds' Pentad (adds hypotension and altered mental status).
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: USG shows dilated CBD (>6mm) and stones; LFTs show conjugated hyperbilirubinemia & ALP > 3x. Management: IV fluids, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, urgent ERCP sphincterotomy/stenting.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Embolism (atrial fibrillation, post-MI) or acute thrombosis on pre-existing atherosclerosis.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Sudden cessation of arterial perfusion resulting in tissue hypoxia, muscle ischemia, and nerve damage within 6 hours.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: The 6 Ps: Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Paresthesia, Paralysis, Perishingly cold. Red Flag: Muscle rigidity and complete sensory loss.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Handheld Doppler / CT Angiography. Management: IV Heparin bolus, emergency Fogarty catheter embolectomy or arterial bypass surgery.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Squamous Cell (tobacco, alcohol, caustic stricture) or Adenocarcinoma (GERD, Barrett's esophagus).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Malignant transmural invasion lacking serosal barrier, leading to early mediastinal and lymphatic dissemination.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Progressive dysphagia (solids then liquids), rapid weight loss, anorexia. Red Flag: Odynophagia, hoarseness, supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Flexible Upper GI Endoscopy (OGDS) with biopsy; CT staging. Management: Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy + Esophagectomy (Ivor Lewis) or SEMS stenting.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Blunt trauma to left lower chest/flank (RTAs, assault, direct kick).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Laceration of splenic parenchyma/capsule causing intra-abdominal hemorrhage and phrenic nerve irritation.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Severe LUQ pain, peritonitis, Kehr's sign (left shoulder tip pain), Ballance's sign (fixed left flank dullness). Red Flag: Hemodynamic instability.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: FAST ultrasound scan / CT Abdomen. Management: Resuscitation (ATLS), emergency exploratory laparotomy and splenectomy; post-splenectomy vaccines.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Protrusion of small bowel/omentum through narrow femoral canal below inguinal ligament (elderly females).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Tight femoral ring causes mechanical neck compression, venous congestion, ischemia, and small bowel obstruction.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Colicky abdominal pain, bilious vomiting, distension, absolute constipation, small tender groin swelling below inguinal ligament.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Plain abdominal X-ray (distended small bowel loops, air-fluid levels). Management: NBM, IV hydration, RTS, emergency groin repair & bowel resection if gangrenous.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Biphasic stromal-epithelial tumor occurring in adult females.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Rapid stromal expansion causing massive breast enlargement, skin stretching, and pressure necrosis.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Large (>5 cm), firm, mobile, bosselated breast mass. Red Flag: Pressure ischemia with ulceration of overlying skin.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Breast USG/Mammography & Core needle biopsy. Management: Wide local excision with >1 cm clear margins or simple mastectomy (no routine axillary dissection).

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Ductal adenocarcinoma of pancreatic head or periampullary region.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Insidious compression and gradual obliteration of the retropancreatic common bile duct causing severe extrahepatic cholestasis.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Painless, continuously progressive obstructive jaundice, severe pruritus, dark urine, clay-colored (acholic) stools, weight loss. Courvoisier's sign.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: LFTs (conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, ALP > 3-5x); CA 19-9; Multiphase CT. Management: Whipple's procedure (Pancreaticoduodenectomy) or ERCP biliary stenting.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Obstructed appendiceal lumen (fecalith, lymphoid hyperplasia) with secondary bacterial infection.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Luminal distension, venous congestion, ischemia, gangrene, and localized or generalized perforation.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Migratory pain (periumbilical to RIF), anorexia, nausea, fever (38°C), localized RIF tenderness, rigidity, rebound tenderness (McBurney's point).
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Ultrasound Abdomen / FBC (leucocytosis). Management: Emergency open or laparoscopic appendectomy & IV antibiotics.

Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Intra-acinar zymogen activation causing auto-digestion, parenchymal necrosis, hemorrhage, and systemic inflammatory response (SIRS).
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, vomiting, paralytic ileus. Red Flag: Periumbilical ecchymosis (Cullen's sign) & flank ecchymosis (Grey Turner's sign).
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Serum Lipase (>3x upper limit of normal, more sensitive/specific than amylase); CT Abdomen. Management: Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation, analgesia, NBM.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Blunt head trauma (temporal bone fracture) tearing the middle meningeal artery.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Arterial bleeding expanding rapidly between inner table of skull and dura mater, elevating intracranial pressure and causing brain herniation.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Transient loss of consciousness followed by a 'lucid interval', then rapid deterioration, severe headache, ipsilateral dilated pupil.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Non-contrast CT Head (biconvex/lenticular hyperdense extra-axial mass). Management: Immediate hypertonic saline/mannitol, emergency burr hole / craniotomy.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Acute venous thrombosis of the inferior hemorrhoidal plexus below the dentate line (triggered by heavy lifting/straining).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Subcutaneous hematoma formation under sensitive squamous epithelium of the anal verge.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Sudden onset of excruciating perianal pain, visible olive-shaped, tense, blue subcutaneous swelling at anal margin.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Clinical inspection. Management: Stool softeners, analgesia, warm sitz baths, or emergency excision under local anesthesia within 48-72 hours.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Nodular hyperplasia of prostatic transition zone driven by dihydrotestosterone (DHT) in aging males.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Mechanical bladder outlet obstruction causing progressive LUTS and risk of acute urinary retention (AROU).
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Frequency, nocturia, hesitancy, weak stream, terminal dribbling, sensation of incomplete emptying. Red Flag: Painful inability to void (AROU).
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Digital Rectal Exam (smooth, firm, enlarged prostate); PSA; Uroflowmetry. Management: Alpha-blockers (Tamsulosin) for quick relief; Finasteride (5-ARI) to shrink prostate and prevent retention.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Thermal and toxic chemical exposure from smoke inhalation in confined spaces.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Thermal injury to upper airway causing rapid edema/stridor; chemical injury to lower respiratory tract causing bronchospasm and ARDS.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Soot in oropharynx/nasal cavity, singed nasal hairs, carbonaceous sputum, hoarseness, stridor, disorientation.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Fiberoptic bronchoscopy; Arterial Blood Gas (Carboxyhemoglobin level). Management: 100% humidified oxygen, early elective endotracheal intubation, ICU support.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Trauma from hard stool evacuation causing an ischemic longitudinal tear in distal anal canal (most common in females).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Hypertonia of internal anal sphincter leading to local ischemia and severe pain, preventing mucosal healing.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Sharp, tearing, excruciating pain during and immediately after defecation, accompanied by bright red blood on toilet paper.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Visual inspection (gently parting buttocks; DRE avoided in acute phase). Management: High-fiber diet, stool softeners, warm sitz baths, topical 0.2% GTN / Diltiazem.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Chronic abnormal epithelialized tract connecting anal canal to perianal skin (following perianal abscess drainage).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Cryptoglandular infection of anal glands spreading along intersphincteric planes.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Recurrent purulent or serosanguinous perianal discharge, localized itching, pain, and a palpable perianal skin opening.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Pelvic MRI (gold standard for mapping complex sphincter relation). Management: Goodsall's rule evaluation; Seton placement, Fistulotomy, or LIFT procedure.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Extra-articular fracture of distal radius within 2.5 cm of wrist joint caused by fall on an outstretched hand (FOOSH).
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Dorsal displacement, dorsal tilt, lateral tilt, and supination of distal radial fragment.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Pain, swelling, tenderness over distal radius, classic 'dinner-fork' deformity.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Plain X-rays of wrist (AP and Lateral views). Management: Closed reduction under hematoma block, immobilization in plaster cast (Colles' cast) for 4-6 weeks.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Complication of severe H. pylori infection or chronic NSAID use.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Transmural ulceration through anterior wall of first part of duodenum, leaking acidic gastric contents into peritoneal cavity.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Sudden onset of agonizing generalized abdominal pain, board-like abdominal rigidity, absent bowel sounds, obliteration of liver dullness.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Erect Chest X-ray (pneumoperitoneum / free gas under diaphragm). Management: Emergency resuscitation, IV fluids, IV PPI, broad-spectrum antibiotics, Cellan-Jones / Graham patch repair.

Key Characteristics & Etiology: Calcium oxalate/phosphate stones formed due to dehydration, hypercalciuria, or metabolic imbalances.
Primary Mechanism & Pathophysiology: Calculus impaction at pelviureteric junction, vesicoureteric junction, or iliac vessel crossing, causing ureteric spasm and obstruction.
Clinical Manifestations & Red Flags: Severe sudden colicky flank pain radiating to the groin/scrotum/labia, restlessness, macroscopic or microscopic hematuria.
Diagnostic Markers & Primary Management: Non-contrast CT KUB (gold standard) / Renal Ultrasound. Management: Analgesia (NSAIDs/morphine), hydration, medical expulsive therapy (Tamsulosin) or ESWL / Ureteroscopy (URS).
